title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context (Problem 1, earlier pages): find an odd curve y(x) through the points x = 0, ±a, ±b, ±c, … with y = 0, ±p, ±q, ±r, …. Euler writes it in Newton divided-difference form in the variable x², y = Ax + Bx(x²−a²) + Cx(x²−a²)(x²−b²) + …. Problem 2 takes p = sin a, q = sin b, …. Letting x → 0 gives 1 = A − Ba² + Ca²b² − …, and the coefficient of each p/a, q/b, … becomes a series.

On p.164 Euler shows that each of these series telescopes. The partial sums of 1 + a²/(b²−a²) + a²b²/((b²−a²)(c²−a²)) + … are b²/(b²−a²), then b²c²/((b²−a²)(c²−a²)), and so on. So the coefficient of p/a is the product Π_{j≠1} a_j²/(a_j²−a_1²), and likewise for the others. The result is
1 = Σ_i (p_i/a_i) Π_{j≠i} a_j²/(a_j²−a_i²).
If the arcs a_i are known rational multiples of π, this is an equation that determines π.

Corollary 1 (§8): with finitely many arcs one gets an approximation. It improves as the arcs become more numerous and closer together, and in the limit of infinitely many arcs gives the exact value.

Corollary 2 (§9): for general x,
sin x / x = Σ_i (p_i/a_i) Π_{j≠i} (a_j²−x²)/(a_j²−a_i²).

Corollary 3 (§10): the same holds for arbitrary data. The odd interpolant through (0,0), (±a_i, ±p_i) is
y/x = Σ_i (p_i/a_i) Π_{j≠i} (a_j²−x²)/(a_j²−a_i²).
This is the Lagrange interpolation formula applied to y/x as a polynomial in x², with nodes a_i². Euler remarks that the form makes visible how each condition is satisfied.

The Scholion (§11, continued on p.166) passes over the finite cases, except for the 4-node approximation to π, and announces infinite node sets in arithmetic progression. Example 1 there takes nodes kΦ and recovers Φ/2 = Σ (−1)^{k+1} sin kΦ / k.
errors: Corollary 1 asserts without qualification that letting the number of arcs grow without bound yields the true ratio. This is not true in general: polynomial interpolation need not converge as nodes are added (Runge-type phenomena).

For the equispaced nodes kΦ used next, the limit formula is valid only for |Φ| < π. At Φ = π every datum sin kπ = 0, so the formula gives 0 instead of π/2. This is exactly the Nyquist-rate failure of sampling sin x at spacing π.
No convergence check of the infinite products and sums is given. This is typical for Euler.

ideas.what: Telescoping the Newton divided-difference coefficients (evaluated at x=0) into closed product form
ideas.modern_name: Conversion of Newton form to Lagrange form of the interpolating polynomial
ideas.where_published: This paper, E555 (1783). Historians of interpolation (e.g. Meijering's chronology) list Euler 1783 alongside Waring and Lagrange.

ideas.what: Interpolation formula for odd functions with nodes ±a_i, using variable x²
ideas.modern_name: Lagrange interpolation in x² for y/x (symmetric/odd interpolation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Waring 1779 / Lagrange 1795 for the general formula

ideas.what: Determining π from sines of known arcs via the interpolant's derivative at 0
ideas.modern_name: Numerical differentiation at x=0 of an interpolant of sin; quadrature-like π approximations

ideas.what: Infinite-node limit of the Lagrange product formula (with nodes kΦ, used on the next page)
ideas.modern_name: Cardinal (Whittaker–Kotelnikov–Shannon) interpolation series, odd case: y(x) = Σ_k y(kΦ)[sinc(x/Φ−k) − sinc(x/Φ+k)]
ideas.usually_credited_to: E.T. Whittaker 1915 (precursors Borel 1897, Cauchy, de la Vallée Poussin)
ideas.where_published: Implicit in E555 §9 combined with Example 1 (§12)

missed.claim: Corollary 2 (§9) with the equispaced infinite nodes a_k = kΦ of Example 1 is precisely the cardinal sampling series for an odd function. Using Π_{j≠k}(1−x²/j²Φ²) = sin(πx/Φ)/[(πx/Φ)(1−x²/k²Φ²)] and Π_{j≠k}(1−k²/j²) = (−1)^{k+1}/2, Euler's formula becomes y(x) = Σ_k y(kΦ)·(−1)^k·2k·sin(πx/Φ) / (π(x²/Φ²−k²)). This equals Σ_k y(kΦ)[sinc(x/Φ−k) − sinc(x/Φ+k)]. Euler's Fourier series Φ/2 = Σ(−1)^{k+1} sin kΦ / k is the x→0 derivative of this sampling expansion of sin x. It holds exactly when Φ < π (sampling above the Nyquist rate) and fails at Φ = π. Euler's route (Lagrange interpolation with infinitely many nodes) is the same route later taken by Borel and Whittaker. I am not aware of E555 being cited as a precursor in the sampling-theorem histories (Higgins, Butzer–Stens et al.), though I am unsure.
missed.quote: Aucto autem arcuum propositorum numero in infinitum, vera ratio peripheriae ad diametrum inde deriuabitur.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It would place an implicit form of the cardinal interpolation series, together with its link to a Fourier series, in 1783. That is more than a century before Borel and Whittaker. It also gives a historically early instance where the band-limit condition (Φ < π for sin x) silently governs validity.

missed.claim: Euler asserts convergence as the nodes multiply but never examines when it holds. The Φ = π counterexample is implicit in his own data, so the question of conditions for convergence of infinite-node interpolation is left open here.
missed.quote: quo maior fit ille numerus, et simul quo minores arcus inter eos occurrant
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is mainly of historical interest. The problem was later settled by Runge/Faber (failure of polynomial interpolation) and by sampling theory (the band-limit condition).

deep.surprise_reason: The Lagrange-form telescoping is a known Euler priority item (Waring 1779, Euler 1783, Lagrange 1795) and is routine in substance. The less-noticed point is that the infinite-node version on this page, combined with Example 1, is effectively the cardinal series for odd functions, with the Nyquist condition implicit. I am not sure the sampling-theory histories credit E555 for this.
transcription_corrections: 'prodit \frac{rbbcc}{(bb-aa)(cc-aa)}' should read 'prodit \frac{bbcc}{(bb-aa)(cc-aa)}'; the 'r' is an OCR artifact.
'quartus adiunctus praebet \frac{sbbccdd}{...}' should read '\frac{bbccdd}{(bb-aa)(cc-aa)(dd-aa)}'; the 's' is spurious.
'si tertius adiatur' should read 'si tertius addatur'.

The second series in the image is written '−\frac{q}{b}\cdot\frac{aa}{bb-aa}\cdot\frac{cc}{cc-bb}\cdots'. It is equivalent to the '+\frac{q}{b}\cdot\frac{aa}{aa-bb}\cdots' form used in the final equation.
